core.name: derive

tsdoc.title: Creates a read-only live signal from a synchronous evaluator.
tsdoc.summary:
The evaluator runs immediately. Signals read during that call become fixed
dependencies whose later changes synchronously recompute the derived value.
Downstream effects run only when the computed output changes by strict equality.
remarks:
- Assigning to `value` is ignored at runtime.
- The first evaluator call receives `undefined`.
- Dependency collection is initial-only and uses a single global effect slot.
- Calling `dispose()` twice throws through the internal effect.

core.name: dispose

tsdoc.title: Disposes derived signals and effects in argument order.
tsdoc.summary:
The function invokes `dispose()` synchronously on every supplied value. An
empty argument list is a valid no-op.
remarks:
- Effect and derived-signal cleanup is immediate.
- Effects are not idempotent: disposing the same effect twice throws.
- If one argument throws during disposal, later arguments are not processed.

core.name: effect

tsdoc.title: Creates an effect and runs its callback immediately.
tsdoc.summary:
Reads of signal `value` properties during the initial callback execution
become permanent stimulus dependencies. Changes to those signals rerun the
callback synchronously until the returned effect is disposed.
remarks:
- Dependency collection occurs only during the initial execution.
- Dependencies skipped by the initial control-flow path are never added later.
- Dependencies collected initially are not removed when later runs skip them.
- Disposal immediately unsubscribes from every stimulus signal.
- Callback errors propagate; the global collection slot is still cleared after an initial error.

params.name: signalsCatcherFn
params.description: The callback to execute and initially inspect for signal reads.

see: {@link dispose} - Disposes multiple effects or derived signals.

tsdoc.title: Creates logical methods for signals.
tsdoc.summary:
Builds the `or`, `is`, and `if` method groups shared by supported signal
values. Comparison results follow the liveness of the input at runtime.
remarks:
- `or()` selects its alternative for every JavaScript-falsy input value
- `is` methods return boolean signals matching the input's liveness
- `if` methods return a `then()` selector for reactive conditional values
- Length comparisons are exposed for strings and arrays
- Measure comparisons are exposed for numbers

```typescript

const logical = getGenericMethods<"live", number>(count);
logical.is.truthy().value; // true
logical.is.greaterThan(3).value; // true
logical.if.greaterThan(10).then("big", "small").value; // "small"
```

core.name: signal

tsdoc.title: Creates a mutable live signal from a JavaScript value.
tsdoc.summary:
The signal tracks effects that read its `value`, stores the previous value on
change, and runs registered effects synchronously. Its value-specific method
surface is selected once at creation time.
remarks:
- Strict-equal assignments are skipped and log an unnecessary-change diagnostic.
- The initial value and values returned by `value` are copied by `@cyftec/immut`.
- The helper set does not change if the value's runtime type changes later.
- Object and array mutations are available under `mutate`, not as direct methods.

params.name: nonNullableInitialValue

tsdoc.summary:
Every argument is unwrapped with `value()` inside a derived evaluator, then
passed to `computerFn` in order. Live argument reads therefore become the
computation's initial dependencies.
remarks:
- The computation runs immediately through `derive()`.
- Plain and dead arguments do not cause future recomputation.
- Dependency collection follows `derive` and is limited to the initial call.
- Errors thrown by `computerFn` propagate synchronously.

the complete chain and tracks live values read on its first evaluation.
remarks:
- `or`, `orNot`, `and`, and `andNot` preserve JavaScript operand semantics.
- Strict equality is used by equality operations.
- JavaScript short-circuiting can skip a signal on the first terminal evaluation; such a signal is not added later.
- Every access to `result`, `truthy`, `falsy`, or `truthyFalsyPair` creates a distinct derived signal.

The input is evaluated once for dispatch: numbers receive arithmetic methods,
strings and arrays receive length methods, and every other value receives the
generic logical surface.
remarks:
- A function input is invoked once immediately for dispatch and again by terminal evaluation.
- The selected operation variant never changes if a live input later changes runtime type.
- Chain methods are lazy; terminal getters and `then()` create derived signals.
- Runtime dispatch uses `typeof` for numbers and strings and `Array.isArray` for arrays.

tsdoc.title: Creates reactive result, error, and pending state for a promise function.
tsdoc.summary:
The returned runner marks the operation as running before invoking
`promiseFn`. Settlement updates a shared state signal whose properties are
exposed as three derived signals.
remarks:
- `isRunning` becomes `true` synchronously when the runner is called and `false` on fulfillment or handled rejection.
- Success replaces the result and clears the prior error.
- Rejection is handled into the error signal and preserves the prior result.
- Rejected values are stored without runtime validation despite the `Error` type annotation.
- A synchronous throw before `promiseFn` returns a promise leaves `isRunning` true and escapes the runner.
- Concurrent runs share one boolean and use settlement order rather than request identity.

A single effect immediately copies the transmitter into each receiver in
argument order and repeats that ordered broadcast when a live transmitter changes.
remarks:
- Receiver initialization is synchronous during this call.
- Plain and dead transmitters perform only the immediate broadcast.
- Receivers remain independently mutable between broadcasts.
- Passing no receivers creates an effect with no signal dependencies.

params.description: The plain value or signal whose value is broadcast.

params.name: receivers
params.description: Source signals to update in argument order.

returns: The disposable effect controlling the broadcast.
see: {@link receive} - Connects several transmitters to one receiver.

tsdoc.title: Unwraps a tuple of signal-capable method arguments.
tsdoc.summary:
Data-specific helpers use this function to convert their plain, live-signal,
and dead-signal operands into the native argument tuple expected by JavaScript.
remarks:
- Live signal arguments participate in dependency collection.
- Dead signals and plain values do not create future updates.
- Function arguments remain functions because `MaybeSignalValues` preserves callable entries.
- The returned array preserves input order.

params.description: Arguments to unwrap in order.

returns: A new array containing each argument's plain value.

utils.name: value
utils.signature:
export const value = <T>(input: MaybeSignal<T> | BaseSignal<T>): T =>
  valueIsSignal(input) ? ((input as BaseSignal<T>).value as T) : (input as T);

tsdoc.title: Unwraps a signal-capable input to its plain value.
tsdoc.summary:
Structurally recognized source, derived, and dead signals are read through
their `value` getter; every other input is returned unchanged.
remarks:
- Reading a live signal through this helper participates in dependency collection.
- Signal getters return copied object and array values according to base-signal behavior.
- `null` and `undefined` pass through unchanged.
- Recognition relies only on the `type` discriminator.
examples:
```typescript
const count = signal(42);
const snapshot = deadSignal("hello");
console.log(value(count)); // 42
console.log(value(snapshot)); // "hello"
console.log(value(null)); // null
```

params.name: input
params.description: A plain value or any base/supported signal shape.

returns: The signal's current value or the original plain input.
see: {@link MaybeSignal} - Describes the general accepted input.
{@link BaseSignal} - Describes the additional low-level input shape.

template.name: T
template.description: The unwrapped value type.

utils.name: valueIsDeadSignal

tsdoc.title: Checks for a dead-signal discriminator and optional value `typeof` filters.
tsdoc.summary:
A matching discriminator is required first. When a non-empty filter list is
supplied, at least one entry must equal `typeof input.value`.
remarks:
- An omitted or empty filter list accepts every dead-signal value type.
- Arrays and null use JavaScript's `"object"` `typeof` result.
- The check is structural and reads `value` only when a type filter is present.
- Nullish and ordinary values return `false`.
examples:
```typescript
const snapshot = deadSignal(42);
valueIsDeadSignal(snapshot); // true
valueIsDeadSignal(snapshot, ["number"]); // true
valueIsDeadSignal(snapshot, ["string"]); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

params.name: shouldMatchAnyOfTypes
params.description: Optional `typeof` strings accepted for the wrapped value.

returns: Whether the discriminator and optional type filter match.
see: {@link valueIsSignal} - Accepts live and dead signals.

utils.name: valueIsDeadSignalString
utils.signature:
export const valueIsDeadSignalString = (input: any): boolean =>
  valueIsDeadSignal(input, ["string"]);

tsdoc.title: Checks for a dead signal whose wrapped value has string `typeof`.
tsdoc.summary:
This convenience guard delegates to `valueIsDeadSignal` with a single
`"string"` value-type filter.
remarks:
- Plain strings and live string signals return `false`.
- The check reads a matching dead signal's `value` for the type comparison.
- Runtime recognition remains structural rather than branded.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsDeadSignalString(deadSignal("text")); // true
valueIsDeadSignalString("text"); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

returns: `true` only for a structurally recognized dead string signal.
see: {@link valueIsDeadSignal} - Performs the discriminator and type check.
{@link DeadSignal} - Represents the accepted signal kind.

utils.name: valueIsDeadSignalStringArray
utils.signature:
export const valueIsDeadSignalStringArray = (input: any): boolean =>
  input?.type === "dead-signal" &&
  Array.isArray(input?.value) &&
  (input?.value as any[]).every((item) => typeof item === "string");

tsdoc.title: Checks for a dead signal containing only string array elements.
tsdoc.summary:
The discriminator and `Array.isArray` must match, then every element is
validated with `typeof item === "string"`.
remarks:
- Empty arrays pass because `Array.prototype.every` is vacuously true.
- Mixed and non-string arrays return `false`.
- Plain and live string arrays return `false`.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsDeadSignalStringArray(deadSignal(["a", "b"])); // true
valueIsDeadSignalStringArray(deadSignal([])); // true
valueIsDeadSignalStringArray(["a"]); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

returns: `true` for dead string arrays, including empty arrays.
see: {@link valueIsDeadSignalString} - Checks a scalar dead string.
{@link DeadSignal} - Represents the accepted signal kind.

tsdoc.title: Checks for the derived-signal runtime discriminator.
tsdoc.summary:
This structural guard tests only whether `input?.type` equals
`"derived-signal"`; it does not validate computation or disposal members.
remarks:
- Source signals, dead signals, nullish values, and ordinary values return `false`.
- A plain object can satisfy this check by carrying the matching discriminator.
- The check does not read `value` and therefore does not collect dependencies.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsDerivedSignal(derive(() => 1)); // true
valueIsDerivedSignal(signal(1)); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

returns: `true` for the derived discriminator and `false` otherwise.

tsdoc.title: Checks whether a value carries either live-signal discriminator.
tsdoc.summary:
Source and derived discriminator strings are accepted; dead signals and all
other values are rejected.
remarks:
- The check is structural and does not validate other signal members.
- Dead signals intentionally return `false`.
- The check does not read `value` and therefore does not collect dependencies.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsLiveSignal(signal(1)); // true
valueIsLiveSignal(deadSignal(1)); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

returns: `true` for a structurally recognized source or derived signal.

utils.name: valueIsMaybeSignalValueOfStringOrArray
utils.signature:
export const valueIsMaybeSignalValueOfStringOrArray = (input: any): boolean =>
  typeof value(input) === "string" || Array.isArray(value(input));

tsdoc.title: Checks whether an unwrapped input is a string or an array.
tsdoc.summary:
The helper calls `value()` and accepts either string `typeof` or
`Array.isArray` on the resulting plain value.
remarks:
- Empty arrays return `true`.
- Nullish, numeric, boolean, and object values return `false`.
- Live signal inputs are read reactively and can be collected as dependencies.
- The implementation unwraps separately for each half of the boolean expression.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsMaybeSignalValueOfStringOrArray(signal("text")); // true
valueIsMaybeSignalValueOfStringOrArray(deadSignal([1])); // true
valueIsMaybeSignalValueOfStringOrArray(1); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: A plain value or structurally recognized signal to inspect.

returns: `true` when the unwrapped value is a string or any array.
see: {@link valueIsSignal} - Checks signal structure without unwrapping.

utils.name: valueIsSignal
utils.signature:
export const valueIsSignal = (input: any): boolean =>
  valueIsLiveSignal(input) || valueIsDeadSignal(input);

tsdoc.title: Checks whether a value carries any supported signal discriminator.
tsdoc.summary: The result combines the live-signal and dead-signal structural checks.
remarks:
- Plain and nullish values return `false`.
- The check does not validate getters, methods, or signal provenance.
- No signal `value` is read when no dead-signal type filter is requested.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsSignal(signal(1)); // true
valueIsSignal(deadSignal(1)); // true
valueIsSignal(1); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

returns: `true` for source, derived, or dead discriminator values.
see: {@link valueIsLiveSignal} - Checks source and derived signals.

tsdoc.title: Checks for the source-signal runtime discriminator.
tsdoc.summary:
This structural guard tests only whether `input?.type` equals
`"source-signal"`; it does not validate the rest of the signal interface.
remarks:
- Derived signals, dead signals, nullish values, and ordinary values return `false`.
- A plain object can satisfy this check by carrying the matching discriminator.
- The check does not read `value` and therefore does not collect dependencies.
examples:
```typescript
valueIsSourceSignal(signal(1)); // true
valueIsSourceSignal(derive(() => 1)); // false
```

params.name: input
params.description: The value to inspect.

returns: `true` for the source discriminator and `false` otherwise.

core.name: BaseDeadSignal

tsdoc.title: Defines the read-only base shape for a non-live signal snapshot.
tsdoc.summary:
This shape reuses the derived base members but changes the discriminator to
`type: "dead-signal"`.
remarks:
- The type does not imply reactive recomputation.
- `DeadSignal` adds generic and value-specific snapshot helpers.

```typescript
declare const snapshot: BaseDeadSignal<string>;
const kind = snapshot.type; // "dead-signal"
```

discriminator is replaced with `type: "derived-signal"`.

- Other low-level base members remain structurally present.
- `DerivedSignal` adds generic and value-specific read helpers.

signal storage interface and discriminator remain important.
remarks:
- Source members expose a writable value.
- Derived members expose a readonly value.

core.name: DeadSignal

tsdoc.title: Represents a read-only, non-reactive signal snapshot.
tsdoc.summary:
A dead signal provides the same value-oriented read helpers as a compatible
live signal, but helper results are further dead snapshots rather than
reactive derived signals.
remarks:
- Its discriminator is `type: "dead-signal"`.
- Assigning to `value` is ignored.
- `dispose()` is a repeatable no-op.
- Signal arguments supplied to its helpers are read once when the helper is called.

template.name: T
template.description: The wrapped value type.

core.name: DerivedOrDeadSignal
core.signature: export type DerivedOrDeadSignal<T> = DerivedSignal<T> | DeadSignal<T>;

tsdoc.title: Represents a read-only result that may be live or a dead snapshot.
tsdoc.summary:
Data and generic helpers use this union when the input is itself a union of
live and dead signals, so the runtime result kind cannot be narrowed further.
remarks:
- The derived branch updates from live dependencies.
- The dead branch remains fixed at creation.

template.name: T
template.description: The result value type.

core.name: DerivedSignal

tsdoc.title: Represents a read-only live signal computed from initial dependencies.
tsdoc.summary:
Derived signals combine a read-only value with generic helpers and
type-specific non-mutating methods. Helper results remain live and are
represented by further derived signals.
remarks:
- Dependencies are the signals read during the evaluator's initial execution.
- Later executions neither add nor remove dependencies.
- `prevValue` contains the previous computed output after an actual output change.
- Disposal immediately disconnects the internal effect and leaves the last value readable.
see: {@link SourceSignal} - Represents a mutable live signal.

template.name: T
template.description: The computed value type.

core.name: DerivedValueGetterWithSignals
core.signature: export type DerivedValueGetterWithSignals<T> = (oldValue: T | undefined) => T;

tsdoc.title: Describes the evaluator accepted by `derive`.
tsdoc.summary:
The evaluator receives the prior computed output and returns the next output.
Signal values read on its first call become the derived signal's dependencies.
remarks:
- `oldValue` is not a previous dependency value.
- Dependencies missed on the first call are not collected on later calls.
- Throwing propagates to the caller that caused the evaluation.

params.name: oldValue
params.description: The previous computed output, or `undefined` on the first call.

returns: The next computed output.

template.description: The value returned by the evaluator.

examples:

```typescript
type LiveNumber = DeriverReturnType<"live", number>; // DerivedSignal<number>
type DeadNumber = DeriverReturnType<"non-live", number>; // DeadSignal<number>
```

core.name: Effect

tsdoc.title: Describes a runnable and disposable reactive effect.
tsdoc.summary:
An effect records stimulus signals read during its initial execution and can
also record dependent signals created by that execution. Its methods expose
execution, registration, and immediate cleanup behavior.
remarks:
- `run()` does nothing after disposal.
- `dependentSignals` is the live internal set and is cleared by disposal.
- Registering signals after disposal throws.
- Calling `dispose()` more than once throws.
see: {@link effect} - Creates and initially runs an effect.
{@link dispose} - Disposes several effects or derived signals.

This discriminator controls whether projection methods return reactive

core.name: IsAndIfComparison
core.signature:
export type IsAndIfComparison<
  InputSignal extends InputSignalType,
  T extends Primitive | any[],
> = {
  is: ([T] extends [Primitive] ? Comparison<InputSignal, "deriver", T> : {}) &
    ([string] extends [T]
      ? LengthComparison<InputSignal, "deriver">
      : [any[]] extends [T]
        ? LengthComparison<InputSignal, "deriver">
        : {});
  if: ([T] extends [Primitive] ? Comparison<InputSignal, "ternary", T> : {}) &
    ([string] extends [T]
      ? LengthComparison<InputSignal, "ternary">
      : [any[]] extends [T]
        ? LengthComparison<InputSignal, "ternary">
        : {});
};

tsdoc.title: Defines direct and ternary comparison groups for a supported value.
tsdoc.summary:
The `is` group returns direct result signals, while the `if` group returns
`then()` continuations. Length groups are added for strings and arrays.
remarks:
- Numeric primitives include ordered comparisons
- Strings and arrays include nested `length` comparisons
see: {@link LengthComparison} - The string and array length group

    ? false

tsdoc.summary:
Produces `true` for object types other than arrays and functions, and `false`
for all remaining types.

- Readonly arrays are excluded together with mutable arrays
- Class instances still satisfy the structural object branch
examples:

core.name: IsUnionAndHasOtherTypeThan
core.signature:
export type IsUnionAndHasOtherTypeThan<T, U> = [true] extends [IsExactly<T, U>]
  ? never
  : Extract<T, U> extends never
    ? never
    : Exclude<T, U> extends never
      ? never
      : true;

tsdoc.title: Detects a union that contains a target type and at least one other type.
tsdoc.summary:
Produces `true` only when `T` includes part of `U` without being exactly `U`;
all other cases resolve to `never`.
remarks: - Exact matches and unions with no matching member both resolve to `never`
examples:

tsdoc.title: Describes the logical chain available for every operation input.
tsdoc.summary:

value with signal-capable logical or comparison operands.
remarks:
- Logical operations use native `||`, `&&`, and `!` semantics.
- Equality operations use strict equality and inequality.
- Two-value comparison helpers evaluate their subject and comparison operands.

- Arithmetic methods return another `NumberOperation`.
- Numeric comparisons return `GenericOperation` boolean chains.
- Range bounds are inclusive by default.
- JavaScript numeric edge cases such as `NaN` and division by zero are preserved.
examples:
```typescript
const chain: NumberOperation = op(10).add(2).mul(3);
console.log(chain.result.value); // 36
```

- Runtime `op()` dispatch is based only on the initially evaluated value.
- This type does not make a chain change shape after creation.
examples:
```typescript

type Textual = Operation<string>; // StringAndArrayOperation
```

- `result` preserves the evaluated value with the broad `unknown` type here.
- Boolean getters coerce with JavaScript truthiness.
- `then()` evaluates only the selected option on each run.

- Comparison values may be plain, live, or dead signals.
- `lengthBetween` includes both bounds by default.
- String length follows JavaScript UTF-16 code-unit semantics.

- Signal values are read reactively when the signal is live.
- Nullish expression results are rendered as empty strings.

```typescript

  () => 42,
  null,
];
```
